title: New Disney book raises allegations about Bob Iger
body_md:
An upcoming book about Disney and its former chief executive Bob Iger is attracting attention ahead of its December 1, 2026 release. The House of Mouse, written by longtime Wall Street Journal reporter Robbie Whelan, is described as an unauthorized biography and corporate history. A November 26 report highlights several allegations and accounts contained in advance material from the book.

According to Whelan's account, as relayed in reporting on an advance copy, Iger had an extramarital relationship with an ABC marketing employee in the early 1990s, when he was overseeing ABC Entertainment. The author describes the relationship as consensual and alleges that it resulted in a pregnancy. The employee is not identified in the report. These are allegations attributed to the author, rather than independently established findings or conclusions reached by a court.

Iger reportedly declined to participate in interviews for the book. The outlet reporting the allegations also said it had contacted Disney and Iger for comment. The available report does not include a response from either party. That absence should not be interpreted as confirmation of the author's account, and the book's claims should be evaluated in light of the evidence presented and any subsequent responses.

Another subject covered by Whelan is executive compensation. The book reportedly describes Iger's frustration with negotiations over his employment contract, including a private email from 2014 that the author says was addressed to then Marvel chairman Ike Perlmutter. The report cites a total compensation package of $45.8 million for Iger in 2025, compared with $41.1 million in 2024. Those figures concern total compensation rather than necessarily representing cash salary alone.

Iger served as Disney's chief executive from 2005 to 2020 and returned in 2022 following the departure of Bob Chapek. According to the report, Josh D'Amaro succeeded him in March 2026. Whelan also discusses Chapek's conduct during his leadership of the company, including an alleged remark about Marvel fans at a film premiere.

Beyond the personal allegations, the book offers a potential opportunity to examine executive power, corporate culture and compensation negotiations at a major entertainment company. Its broader value will depend on the quality of its sourcing, the context supplied for individual accounts and its treatment of competing perspectives. Readers should distinguish between documented corporate developments and disputed or unverified personal claims. Publication of the full book may provide additional context, while responses from the people discussed could help clarify the record.
excerpt: Robbie Whelan's unauthorized biography examines Iger and Disney's corporate culture.
